title: Pieces of Asteroids
subtitle: Bringing the sky home
yt_title: What We Found Inside an Asteroid 🧪 | Ep. 112 #shorts
description:
Episode 112 of a daily journey through the universe. 🧪
We open asteroid samples: Japan's Hayabusa2 brought 5.4 g of Ryugu home in 2020, NASA's OSIRIS-REx returned 121.6 g of Bennu in 2023, with 14 of the 20 amino acids life uses, all 5 DNA and RNA bases, salty brine minerals and even sugars.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 113: Next stop, cosmic inflation. The universe's first trillionth of a second.
Start from Episode 1 "Leaving Earth" on the channel.
Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

Images: NASA (public domain)
Narration: AI voice

#space #osirisrex #astronomy #shorts #science #nasa

segments.text: Episode one hundred and twelve. Next stop... pieces of asteroids.
Two spacecraft did something incredible. They touched asteroids, and brought pieces back to Earth.
segments.headline: Touch and go

segments.text: First, Japan's Hayabusa2 visited asteroid Ryugu. In twenty twenty, its capsule landed in Australia with about five grams of asteroid.
Then NASA's OSIRIS-REx grabbed rocks from asteroid Bennu. In twenty twenty-three, it dropped one hundred and twenty-one grams into the Utah desert.
When OSIRIS-REx touched Bennu, the surface acted like a ball pit. The spacecraft sank in, and had to back away fast.
segments.headline: Like a ball pit

segments.text: Inside the Bennu sample, scientists found fourteen of the twenty amino acids life uses to build proteins.
Plus all five bases used in DNA and RNA, salts left by evaporated salty water, and even sugars.
segments.headline: DNA bases and sugars

segments.text: It doesn't mean there was life on Bennu. But the ingredients of life were floating in space before Earth existed.
segments.headline: Ingredients for life

segments.text: Hayabusa2 isn't done. It's on its way to a tiny, fast-spinning asteroid, arriving in twenty thirty-one.
segments.headline: Hayabusa2 flies on

segments.text: Tomorrow, the craziest moment in history. In a tiny fraction of a second, the universe grew from smaller than an atom to the size of a grapefruit. Follow, so you don't miss episode one hundred and thirteen.
